title: Given weights and profits of N items, put a subset of these items into a knapsack of capacity C so that the total profit is maximized, where each item can be used at most once. Explain the 0/1 Knapsack dynamic programming pattern, the table, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: 0/1 Knapsack (Maximize Value Within a Weight Capacity, Each Item Once)

s1_definition.profdef: 0/1 Knapsack is the foundational problem of the 0/1 Knapsack dynamic programming pattern. For each item we make a binary choice, include it or skip it, subject to a capacity constraint, and we maximize total value. The standard solution is a two-dimensional table over items and capacities, or a space-optimized one-dimensional array iterated from high capacity down to low so each item is counted once. Time is N times C and optimized space is C.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India gives Rajesh a fixed investment budget. Each investment has a cost and an expected return and he can either buy it once or not at all. He wants the highest total return without exceeding the budget. 0/1 Knapsack decides, for every budget level, the best return achievable, by asking item by item whether including it beats leaving it out.
s1_definition.oneliner: For each item choose include or skip; a table over items and capacity stores the best value.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** 0/1 Knapsack is the foundational problem of the 0/1 Knapsack dynamic programming pattern. For each item we make a binary choice, include it or skip it, subject to a capacity constraint, and we maximize total value. The standard solution is a two-dimensional table over items and capacities, or a space-optimized one-dimensional array iterated from high capacity down to low so each item is counted once. Time is N times C and optimized space is C.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India gives Rajesh a fixed investment budget. Each investment has a cost and an expected return and he can either buy it once or not at all. He wants the highest total return without exceeding the budget. 0/1 Knapsack decides, for every budget level, the best return achievable, by asking item by item whether including it beats leaving it out.

**One line to remember:** For each item choose include or skip; a table over items and capacity stores the best value.

sections.s2_technical:
The recurrence is the heart of the pattern. For item `i` and capacity `c`, the best value is the larger of two options: skip item `i`, giving the best value using earlier items at the same capacity, or include item `i` if it fits, giving its profit plus the best value using earlier items at capacity `c minus weight[i]`. Formally `dp[i][c] = max(dp[i-1][c], profit[i] + dp[i-1][c - weight[i]])` when `weight[i] <= c`.

The space-optimized version keeps a single array `dp[c]` and iterates capacity from high down to low for each item: `for (int c = C; c >= weight[i]; c--) dp[c] = Math.max(dp[c], profit[i] + dp[c - weight[i]])`. Iterating downward is essential because it ensures each item is used at most once; iterating upward would allow reusing the same item, which is the unbounded variant. Senior nuance: the answer sits at `dp[C]`, and reconstructing which items were chosen requires either the full two-dimensional table or a parallel record of decisions.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India offers Rajesh a set of one-time investment products, each with a rupee cost and an expected return, and a fixed investment budget. He may buy each product at most once. The advisory engine must pick the subset that maximizes expected return without exceeding the budget. This is exactly how 0/1 Knapsack works: each product is an include-or-skip decision under a capacity limit.

The code defines a `PortfolioKnapsackService` exposing `maxReturn(costs, returns, budget)` that returns the best achievable return. A `Demo` runs it over a small product set and logs the maximum return within budget.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is four products with costs 2, 3, 4, 5 and returns 3, 4, 5, 6, and a budget of five. The dp array has indices zero through five, all starting at zero.

Step 1 — Process product zero, cost two, return three. For capacities five down to two we set dp[c] to the better of its current value and three plus dp[c minus two]. Now dp is 0, 0, 3, 3, 3, 3.

Step 2 — Process product one, cost three, return four. Iterating five down to three, dp[5] becomes max of 3 and 4 plus dp[2] which is 4 plus 3 equals 7; dp[4] becomes max of 3 and 4 plus dp[1] equals 4; dp[3] becomes 4. Now dp is 0, 0, 3, 4, 4, 7.

Step 3 — Process product two, cost four, return five. dp[5] becomes max of 7 and 5 plus dp[1] equals 5, stays 7; dp[4] becomes max of 4 and 5 plus dp[0] equals 5. Now dp is 0, 0, 3, 4, 5, 7.

Step 4 — Process product three, cost five, return six. dp[5] becomes max of 7 and 6 plus dp[0] equals 6, stays 7. The array settles.

Step 5 — The best return within budget five is dp[5], which is seven, achieved by buying products zero and one, costing five and returning seven. The output is below.

```
Oct 27, 2026 8:54:10 PM com.bank.portfolio.service.PortfolioKnapsackService maxReturn
INFO: Max return within budget = 7
Oct 27, 2026 8:54:10 PM com.bank.portfolio.PortfolioKnapsackApplication main
INFO: Best expected return within budget 5 lakh: 7 lakh
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
0/1 Knapsack is the foundational problem of the 0/1 Knapsack dynamic programming pattern. Every item presents a binary choice, include it or skip it, under a shared capacity limit, and I maximize total value. The recurrence says the best value for the current item at a given capacity is the larger of skipping it, which keeps the best value from earlier items at that capacity, or including it when it fits, which adds its profit to the best value from earlier items at the reduced capacity.

The detail that proves I understand the pattern is the space optimization. I collapse the table to a single array indexed by capacity and, for each item, I sweep capacity from high down to low. The downward sweep guarantees each item is counted at most once, because when I update a higher capacity I am reading values that have not yet been touched by the current item. Sweeping upward instead would let the same item be reused, which is the unbounded knapsack variant, so the direction of the loop is a deliberate correctness decision, not a style choice.

At the National Bank of India I used this in an advisory engine that picked one-time investment products for a customer like Rajesh, each product having a cost and an expected return, to maximize total return within his budget. I used the one-dimensional array with the downward capacity sweep and read the answer at the full budget. Explaining the include-or-skip recurrence, the N times C cost, and why the high-to-low sweep enforces the use-each-item-once rule is what shows an interviewer that I truly understand 0/1 Knapsack rather than having memorized a loop.
